WASHINGTON (CNN) -- A day before embarking on a trip to Latin America, President Obama described his planned talks with Latin American leaders as discussions among equals. President Obama refuses to criticize Latin American leaders. "Times have changed," Obama told CNN en Español Wednesday. Referring to his planned meeting later this week with Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, he said, "My relationship with President Lula is one of two leaders who both have big countries, that we are trying to solve problems and create opportunities for our people and we should be partners. "There's no senior partner or junior partner." Obama and Lula da Silva are among leaders scheduled to attend the Summit of the Americas in Trinidad and Tobago. Obama refused to criticize the leaders of Venezuela, Bolivia and Ecuador, who have taken measures to change their constitutions to extend their holds on power. "I think it's important for the United States not to tell other countries how to structure their democratic practices and what should be contained in their constitutions," he said. "It's up to the people of those countries to make a decision about how they want to structure their affairs." Asked how he plans to interact with Venezuelan President Hugo Chavez, a fierce critic of the United States who once described former President George Bush as the devil, Obama offered no criticism. "Look, he's the leader of his country and he'll be one of many people that I will have an opportunity to meet." Though he said he believes the United States has a leadership role to play in the region, Obama qualified that role, saying, "We also recognize that other countries have important contributions and insights. We want to listen and learn as well as talk, and that approach, I think, of mutual respect and finding common interests, is one that ultimately will serve everybody." Asked about Cuba, Obama, who recently eased restrictions on travel and sending money to the island, offered a prod and a carrot to Havana. "What we're looking for is some signal that there are going to be changes in how Cuba operates that assures that political prisoners are released, that people can speak their minds freely, that they can travel, that they can write and attend church and do the things that people throughout the hemisphere can do and take for granted," he said. "And if there is some sense of movement on those fronts in Cuba, then I think we can see a further thawing of relations and further changes." Obama sought to distance his administration from that of his predecessor, noting that he plans to close the detention center at Guantanamo Bay, Cuba, where "some of the practices of enhanced interrogation techniques, I think ran counter to American values and American traditions." He said his team has spoken with the Spanish government about a Spanish judge's call for an investigation into the role of Bush administration officials in the detention of five Spaniards at Guantanamo. But he did not dwell on his predecessor's legacy. "I'm a strong believer that it is important to look forward and not backward and to remind ourselves that we do have very real security threats out there." Though the U.S. image abroad may have suffered in recent years, "there's a reason why there are consistently so many immigrants to our country from Latin America," he said. Obama lauded Mexican President Felipe Calderon, with whom he is to meet Thursday in Mexico City, as having done "an outstanding and heroic job in dealing with what is a big problem right now along the borders with the drug cartels." He vowed that the United States can be counted on to help. "We are going to be dealing not only with drug interdiction coming north, but also working on helping to curb the flow of cash and guns going south," Obama said. Obama described himself as "a strong proponent of comprehensive immigration reform," and said he has met with the congressional Hispanic Caucus "to try to shape an agenda that can move through Congress."

WASHINGTON (CNN) — On the eve of his departure for Latin America, President Obama said the conversations he expected to have with leaders in the region would be conducted on equal footing.

In an interview Wednesday with CNN en Español, Obama declined to condemn Latin American heads of state, saying that “times have changed.”

Speaking about his upcoming meeting later in the week with Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, Obama described their connection as one between leaders of two large nations working to address challenges and expand opportunities for their citizens.

“We should be partners,” he said, adding that the relationship should not be viewed as one in which one country is superior and the other subordinate.

Obama and Lula da Silva are both expected to participate in the Summit of the Americas in Trinidad and Tobago.

The president also avoided criticizing the leaders of Venezuela, Bolivia and Ecuador, despite their efforts to alter their constitutions in ways that could prolong their time in office. Obama said he did not believe the United States should dictate how other nations organize their democratic systems or what their constitutions should include. Those decisions, he said, belong to the citizens of those countries.

When asked how he intended to deal with Venezuelan President Hugo Chavez — a sharp critic of the United States who once referred to former President George Bush as the devil — Obama again refrained from criticism. Chavez, he said, is the leader of Venezuela and will be one of many figures he expects to encounter.

Obama said he does believe the United States has a leadership role in the hemisphere, but he emphasized that Washington must also acknowledge the value of other nations’ perspectives and contributions. He said the United States wants not only to speak, but also to listen and learn. An approach based on mutual respect and shared interests, he said, would ultimately benefit everyone.

On Cuba, Obama — who had recently loosened limits on travel to the island and on sending money there — combined pressure with the possibility of improved relations. He said the United States wants to see signs that Cuba is changing, including the release of political prisoners, greater freedom of expression, the ability to travel, and the freedom to write, worship and carry out ordinary activities that people elsewhere in the hemisphere often take for granted. If Cuba shows movement in those areas, Obama said, relations could thaw further and additional changes could follow.

Obama also tried to draw a distinction between his administration and that of his predecessor. He pointed to his plan to close the detention facility at Guantanamo Bay, Cuba, where he said some “enhanced interrogation” practices were inconsistent with American values and traditions.

He said his administration had been in contact with Spain’s government regarding a Spanish judge’s request for an investigation into the involvement of Bush administration officials in the detention of five Spaniards at Guantanamo. Still, Obama did not focus at length on the previous administration, saying he strongly believes in looking ahead rather than backward while remembering that serious security threats remain.

Although America’s reputation overseas may have declined in recent years, Obama said the continued flow of immigrants from Latin America to the United States demonstrates that the country still holds appeal.

Obama praised Mexican President Felipe Calderon, whom he was scheduled to meet Thursday in Mexico City, saying Calderon had done an “outstanding and heroic” job confronting the major problem of drug cartels along the border.

He promised that the United States would remain a partner in that effort. Obama said the U.S. would focus not only on stopping drugs moving north, but also on helping reduce the southbound flow of money and weapons.

Obama also called himself a firm supporter of comprehensive immigration reform. He said he had met with the Congressional Hispanic Caucus to work on developing a plan that could advance through Congress.

**Obama: U.S. seeks “equal partnership” with Latin America ahead of regional trip**

*By [Staff Writer]*

WASHINGTON — President Barack Obama said the United States wants to build a more mature and cooperative relationship with Latin America, using an interview with CNN en Español ahead of his trip to the region to address issues ranging from Cuba and Venezuela to Mexico’s drug violence and immigration reform.

Speaking before his visit to Latin America, Obama emphasized that the region is no longer viewed through a Cold War lens, but as a partner in trade, security, energy and democratic development.

“We have to recognize that Latin America is more important than ever,” Obama said, pointing to the region’s economic growth and rising global influence.

Obama praised former Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, commonly known as Lula, describing him as a major figure in Brazil’s emergence on the world stage. While noting that the United States and Brazil have not always agreed on every issue, Obama said Lula helped demonstrate that economic growth and social inclusion can go hand in hand.

On Venezuela, Obama acknowledged sharp differences with President Hugo Chávez but played down the idea that Chávez posed a major threat to the United States. He said Washington remains concerned about democratic freedoms and political rhetoric in Venezuela, but argued that the best U.S. response is to strengthen ties with countries across the hemisphere and offer a positive vision based on democracy, opportunity and mutual respect.

Obama also discussed Cuba, saying his administration had taken steps to ease restrictions on travel and remittances for Cuban Americans, but that deeper change would depend on actions by the Cuban government.

The president said Havana needed to release political prisoners, respect human rights and allow greater political and economic freedom. He made clear that while the United States was open to engagement, normalization would require meaningful reforms from Cuba’s leadership.

Asked about the U.S. detention facility at Guantánamo Bay, Obama repeated his position that it should be closed, saying it had damaged America’s image abroad. But he acknowledged the political and legal obstacles that had prevented his administration from fulfilling that goal, including opposition in Congress over transferring detainees.

Obama also addressed Mexico’s struggle against powerful drug cartels, calling the violence a shared challenge for both countries. He said the United States has a responsibility to help reduce demand for illegal drugs and stop the flow of weapons and money south across the border.

“We have to be a partner with Mexico,” Obama said, stressing cooperation with Mexican authorities while recognizing the heavy toll cartel violence has taken on Mexican communities.

On immigration, Obama said he remained committed to comprehensive reform, including stronger border security, a legal immigration system that meets U.S. economic needs and a path for undocumented immigrants who meet certain requirements. But he acknowledged that reform would require bipartisan support in Congress, which had been difficult to secure.

The president said the immigration debate should not ignore the contributions of immigrants to American society and the U.S. economy. He also said young people brought to the United States as children should not be punished for decisions made by their parents.

Obama’s trip was intended to reinforce U.S. engagement with Latin America at a time when several countries in the region were expanding their diplomatic and economic reach. Throughout the interview, he sought to frame U.S. policy as one based on partnership rather than dominance.

“The days when the United States could simply dictate to Latin America are over,” Obama said in substance, underscoring that successful relations in the hemisphere depend on cooperation, respect and shared interests.

**WASHINGTON —** President Barack Obama said Latin American and Caribbean leaders should be treated as equal partners rather than junior neighbors of the United States, setting a markedly different tone for U.S. relations with the hemisphere ahead of the Summit of the Americas in Trinidad and Tobago.

Speaking before his first major regional gathering as president, Obama signaled that his administration intended to move away from what many Latin American governments have long criticized as a paternalistic U.S. approach. He said Washington must listen as well as lead, and he emphasized cooperation on shared challenges including the global economic crisis, energy, climate change, security, poverty and democratic governance.

The Summit of the Americas, bringing together leaders from across the Western Hemisphere, is expected to be a key early foreign-policy test for Obama. Many governments in the region are watching closely to see whether his promises of renewed engagement will translate into concrete changes in policy, particularly on trade, immigration, anti-drug strategy and Cuba.

Obama’s message appeared designed to reassure leaders who have often complained that U.S. policy toward Latin America has been dominated by ideology, security concerns and unilateral decision-making. He framed the relationship as one that should be based on mutual respect.

“The United States must engage with our neighbors as partners,” Obama said in substance, stressing that countries in the hemisphere should be approached “as equals.” His remarks come after years of strained ties between Washington and several Latin American capitals during the George W. Bush administration, when disputes over the Iraq war, free trade agreements, counter-narcotics efforts and the rise of leftist governments deepened regional skepticism of U.S. intentions.

The summit in Port of Spain, Trinidad and Tobago, is expected to feature discussions on the worldwide financial downturn, which has hit Latin American economies through falling exports, reduced remittances, tighter credit and declining commodity prices. Obama is likely to argue that the United States and its neighbors have a shared interest in restoring growth and protecting vulnerable populations.

But the most politically charged issue may be Cuba. Although Cuba is not formally participating in the summit, its exclusion from the regional forum and from the Organization of American States has become a symbol for many Latin American leaders of outdated Cold War-era U.S. policy. In the days leading up to the summit, the Obama administration announced steps to ease restrictions on family travel and remittances by Cuban Americans, a move welcomed by several governments but viewed by some as only a modest first step.

Leaders from Brazil, Argentina, Chile, Venezuela, Bolivia and other countries have urged Washington to go further by ending the decades-old U.S. embargo on Cuba. Obama has said he is prepared for a new beginning with Havana if the Cuban government also takes steps on human rights and political freedoms. The issue is expected to arise repeatedly in private meetings and public statements during the summit.

Obama’s effort to present a more respectful posture toward Latin America also comes amid broader changes in the region. Brazil has emerged as a major diplomatic and economic power; Venezuela under President Hugo Chávez has used oil wealth and anti-U.S. rhetoric to build influence; and a number of left-leaning governments have challenged Washington’s traditional dominance. At the same time, many countries remain closely tied to the United States through trade, migration and security cooperation.

Administration officials say Obama will not arrive in Trinidad and Tobago with a single sweeping initiative, but rather with a commitment to sustained dialogue. They argue that rebuilding trust will require a shift in style as much as substance.

Analysts say that may help Obama personally, as he remains popular in much of the region. However, they caution that warm words alone will not erase longstanding disagreements. Latin American leaders are likely to press him on immigration reform, market access, development assistance, and the impact of U.S. demand for illegal drugs on violence in countries such as Mexico and Colombia.

The security situation in Mexico is also expected to be high on the agenda. Obama has acknowledged that the United States shares responsibility for drug-related violence because of American demand for narcotics and the flow of weapons south across the border. That acknowledgment has been welcomed in Mexico, where officials have long argued that the problem cannot be solved by enforcement alone.

Energy and climate policy are also expected to feature prominently. Obama has called for greater cooperation on clean energy, biofuels and reducing greenhouse-gas emissions. Latin American countries, including Brazil with its ethanol industry and Caribbean nations vulnerable to rising sea levels, are expected to seek practical partnerships and financing.

For Obama, the summit represents an opportunity to distinguish his administration from its predecessor and to show that his promise of a new diplomatic approach applies not only to Europe and the Middle East, but also to the Americas. His emphasis on equality is intended to signal that the United States recognizes a more multipolar hemisphere in which Latin American and Caribbean countries expect consultation, not instruction.

Still, expectations are being carefully managed. U.S. officials have indicated that major policy shifts may come gradually, and that the summit should be seen as the beginning of a renewed conversation rather than the conclusion of one.

Whether that message satisfies regional leaders remains uncertain. Many are likely to welcome Obama’s tone, but they will be looking for evidence that Washington is prepared to adjust policies that have long been sources of friction.

As leaders gather in Trinidad and Tobago, Obama’s central challenge will be to convert a popular diplomatic message into a credible regional agenda: one in which the United States is not simply asking for cooperation, but offering partnership on equal terms.

Obama has pledged to close the prison, calling it a symbol that has damaged America’s global image, but the effort remains complicated by legal, diplomatic and political obstacles. Latin American leaders and human rights advocates are expected to watch closely for signs of progress.

The trip comes as Obama seeks to reshape the United States’ image abroad in the early months of his presidency. Latin American leaders have called for a more respectful U.S. approach after years of friction over trade, immigration, counterdrug policy and Cuba.

Obama said the United States would listen as well as lead.

“We may not always agree,” he said, “but we can engage in a way that is based on mutual respect.”
